title: Karmic tail 15-5-8 in the destiny matrix: tradition, betrayal and trial

seo.title: Karmic tail 15-5-8 in the destiny matrix: “Betrayal in the Family”
seo.description: 15-5-8 is called “Betrayal in the Family”. Why Waite describes the Devil as the Hierophant reversed, how a union becomes a chain, and where the way out is.

short: 15-5-8 is a karmic tail with the Devil at the entry, the Hierophant as the mechanism and Justice at the root. Popular Russian-language readings call it “Betrayal in the Family”. The name is more accurate than it looks, only its sense is different: in Russian, “betrayal” (predatelstvo) and “tradition” (predanie) share a root, and this tail is about how a union, a vow or a family rule quietly turns into a chain, while the reckoning arrives as a trial, outer or inner. The tail is common: about one person in eleven has it.

sections.h2: How to find the 15-5-8 tail from a date of birth
paragraphs: The check takes half a minute and needs no calculator. Add up three numbers from the date of birth:

ol: **The day.** If it is greater than 22, add its digits: 23 → 5, 28 → 10, 31 → 4.
**The month** — as it is, from 1 to 12.
**The year** — the sum of its digits. If that sum is greater than 22, reduce it once more: 1985 → 23 → 5. For 1990 the sum is 19, so nothing needs reducing.

paragraphs: The tail is 15-5-8 exactly when the sum of the three numbers is **26, 35, 44 or 53**. There are no other options: each of these sums reduces to 8, the karmic task, and the centre of the chart then always comes out as 7.

Two examples. 09.12.1985: 9 + 12 + 5 = 26 — the tail is 15-5-8. 28.06.1990: day 28 gives 10, and 10 + 6 + 19 = 35 — 15-5-8 again. The date 15.07.1990, by contrast, gives 15 + 7 + 19 = 41, and its tail is a different one, 15-20-5. The triple 15-5-8 still appears in that chart, only on another line — more on this in the questions at the end.
A sum of exactly 8 also reduces to 8, but it gives a different tail, and the rarest one — 6-14-8: in 127 years there are only 55 such dates.

Across all dates from 1900 to 2026, the 15-5-8 tail occurs in 4,282 cases out of 46,386. That is 9.2% and third place among the 26 possible tails: only 15-20-5 and 12-19-7 are more frequent. The sums 26 and 35 account for 41% of cases each, 44 for 16%, and 53 for about 2%.

sections.h2: Why 15-5-8 is called “Betrayal in the Family”
paragraphs: Popular readings give this tail the name “Betrayal in the Family”, sometimes “Betrayals and Passions in the Family”. They explain it with a past-life legend: love triangles, affairs, broken families. Other versions speak of a spiritual mentor who gave in to temptation, or of someone who abused their power over the people closest to them.

The legend cannot be checked: a date of birth says nothing about past lives. There is also a matter of scale. One person in eleven has this tail. A literal story of a broken family, assigned to that share of people, sounds less like an interpretation than like an accusation. And accusation, as will become clear, is a theme of its own in this tail.

But the name does not rest on the legend alone. It can be assembled from the divinatory lists of Arthur Edward Waite, author of one of the most influential books on tarot (1910). The Hierophant's list opens with “Marriage, alliance, captivity, servitude”. Waite describes the Devil as “the chain and fatality of the material life”. And among the meanings of Justice are the “triumph of the deserving side in law” and, reversed, “legal complications”.

**Marriage, chain, trial.** The legend of family betrayal can be put together almost word for word from the three cards of the tail. Only it comes together differently from the way it is usually retold. The legend speaks of one person who betrayed. The cards describe at least three figures: the one who is bound, the one who keeps the form, and the one who judges. And the most important detail: in Waite, the Devil and the Hierophant are not enemies.

sections.h2: The Devil is the Hierophant reversed
paragraphs: Waite describes the Devil's raised hand as “the reverse of that benediction which is given by the Hierophant in the fifth card”. He compares the Devil not with just any card, but specifically with the Hierophant. In the 15-5-8 tail the two stand side by side: entry and mechanism.

What exactly is reversed? Waite calls the Hierophant's gesture a sign “distinguishing between the manifest and concealed part of doctrine”. From the start, the Hierophant's blessing draws a line between what is shown to everyone and what stays inside. The Devil makes the same gesture in reverse. **The line between the manifest and the hidden remains, but now the hidden rules the manifest.**

The compositions mirror each other too. Before the Hierophant, in Waite's description, two ministers kneel. Before the Devil stand two figures, with chains running from a ring on the altar to their necks. Waite calls this pair “analogous with those of the fifth card” — though he immediately adds “as if Adam and Eve after the Fall”, and in his deck Adam and Eve are on the sixth card, the Lovers. Whether this is a misprint or intended is unknown: the scan of the 1922 edition has the same “fifth”. But the raised hand leaves no doubt, and the two cards share one composition anyway: one figure above, two below. The whole difference is in what binds the lower figures to the upper one — service or a chain.

Captivity is already present in the Hierophant himself. His full list in Waite reads: “Marriage, alliance, captivity, servitude; by another account, mercy and goodness; inspiration; the man to whom the Querent has recourse.” Marriage and captivity stand in the same line. Benebell Wen, author of Holistic Tarot (2015), says the same thing from the other side. To conform, a person has to repress what makes them different from others — “Hence, The Hierophant card is also about concealment.” And of the Devil she writes that it is “related to antagonism and dogma, despotism and enslavement”. Dogma is a word from the Hierophant's vocabulary.

The key phrase of the tail is Waite's line about the Devil himself. He who is exalted above the two figures “is not to be their master for ever. Even now, he is also a bondsman”, “blind to the liberty of service”. The difference between the Hierophant and the Devil is the difference between service and servitude. From outside they look the same: the same loyalty, the same rules, the same person on top. **In the 15-5-8 tail the Devil does not break into the family from outside. He is the family's own form, once it has stopped being free.**

sections.h2: Tradition and betrayal are one word
paragraphs: Russian keeps this knot inside its words. Predatelstvo, “betrayal”, comes from predat — literally “to hand over into someone else's hands”. The same verb gives predanie, “tradition”: what is handed down from generation to generation — family rules, faith, and, in church language, Holy Tradition, the Hierophant's own territory. It also gives the legal phrase predat sudu, “to commit to trial”. In Soviet criminal procedure, predanie sudu was the name of a separate stage: the moment a case was handed over to the court. English keeps a similar pair through Latin: tradere, “to hand over”, gave both tradition and traitor.

The three cards of the tail — tradition (the Hierophant), betrayal (the Devil) and committal to trial (Justice) — are one verb with three meanings. The apostle Paul puts the first two in a single chapter. In the NRSV: “maintain the traditions just as I handed them on to you” (1 Cor 11:2) — and twenty verses later: “the Lord Jesus on the night when he was betrayed took a loaf of bread” (1 Cor 11:23). In the Greek original, “traditions”, “handed on” and “betrayed” all come from one verb, paradidomi, “to hand over”.

The second knot is the word soyuz, “union”. In Old Russian, sŭuzŭ meant at once “fetters, bonds, union, society” (Vasmer's etymological dictionary). Uzy braka, “the bonds of marriage”, and uznik, “prisoner”, share a root. Svyaz, “tie” — a love affair as well as a business connection — comes from vyazat, “to bind”, and so does obyazatelstvo, “obligation”. English “bond” does the same double work, and Waite himself calls the Devil a “bondsman”. By root, language does not tell a union from fetters. The difference lies elsewhere: whether the knot can be untied by hand or has to be cut.

For 15-5-8 this is not wordplay but a description of the plot. What a family hands down as tradition (“that's how we do things”, “in our family people don't divorce”, “we don't wash our dirty linen in public”) may one day turn into betrayal — one's own or someone else's — and then into a trial. The question of this tail is not whether to bind oneself: nobody lives without unions. The question is **which knot is holding**.

The positions of the tail are read according to the classic scheme. The entry (M) is where the plot begins and where it shows first. The mechanism (N) is what keeps the circle turning. The root (D, the karmic task) is the returning question from which everything starts again. In 15-5-8 the circle looks like this (this is our reading of the cards):

ol: **The chain — the Devil at the entry.** An attachment appears that gives an immediate reward and takes away choice: passion, money, approval, a secret arrangement, a debt, dependence on a person or a habit. Wen describes the Devil as a “preference for instant gratification over delayed gratification”.

**The form — the Hierophant as the mechanism.** The chain is hidden under a proper form, or the form itself becomes the chain. “That's how it's done”, “for the children's sake”, “what will people say”. The rules are no longer discussed: they are only obeyed or secretly broken.

**The trial — Justice at the root.** What was hidden comes out, or an account builds up: exposure, divorce, division of property, a family council, a dismissal. Or an inner prosecutor who keeps the case open for years. There is one question: who owes what to whom, and who is right.

**The chain again.** A sentence that is too harsh gives birth to a new prohibition, and the prohibition to a new craving. The condemned goes into exile, the judge becomes a warden. In Waite, the Devil card is life after the verdict: in his words, it signifies “the Dweller on the Threshold without the Mystical Garden when those are driven forth therefrom who have eaten the forbidden fruit”. The circle closes.

paragraphs: The method's formula points to the same logic. The entry of this tail is the sum of the root and the centre: 8 + 7 = 15. The mechanism is the sum of the root and the entry: 8 + 15 = 23, and 2 + 3 = 5. Arithmetic proves nothing, but the picture is telling: **rightness (Justice) driven towards victory (the Chariot) produces a chain (the Devil)**. And rightness and the chain together make up a rule — the Hierophant. Many family “we just don't do that” rules are exactly this alloy: the hardened trace of an old story in which someone was guilty and someone judged.

An important caveat. The circle does not mean that a person will certainly be unfaithful or be cheated on. It describes the shape that difficult stories tend to take for people with this tail — in family, at work, in faith, with money. Where exactly it will show, and whether it will show visibly at all, a date of birth does not say. Even Waite's list for the Devil ends with a caveat: fatality is “that which is predestined but is not for this reason evil”.

sections.h2: The hidden fourth card: everyone with 15-5-8 has the Chariot at the centre
paragraphs: The triple 15-5-8 arises with only one centre of the chart. If the entry is 15 and the root is 8, the centre has to be 7, otherwise the formula does not add up. So every person with this tail has the Chariot at the centre. In the destiny matrix the centre is the comfort zone: what a person returns to by default when things get hard.

Waite describes the Chariot as victory — “He is above all things triumph in the mind” — and as liberation: “He has led captivity captive”. These are words from the Psalms, the same phrase the King James Bible uses. But Waite sets a limit at once. The charioteer's conquests are outward, not inward, and the liberation he brings “may leave himself in the bondage of the logical understanding”.

So Waite writes the word captivity for three of the four cards: the Devil's chain, the captivity and servitude in the Hierophant's list, and the captivity the charioteer has led captive. The fourth card, Justice, is the law. The whole set of the tail is about unfreedom and how it is resolved.

The centre and the root share another word. Among the Chariot's meanings are “war, triumph, presumption, vengeance”, and, reversed, “litigation”. Among the meanings of Justice is the “triumph of the deserving side in law”. Triumph appears in both. Hence, in our reading, the centre's main temptation: **to turn a trial into a war**, where the point is not to restore balance but to win. The second temptation is to leave. When the knot tightens, the Chariot offers a change of city, job, partner, project. Movement brings relief, but the knot travels with the charioteer.

Without the Chariot's strong side, the tail is misread. It is the ability to lead out of captivity — oneself and others. The Chariot does not endure; it acts. If the person holds the reins rather than the grievance, the centre 7 turns 15-5-8 from a story about a chain into a story about liberation.

The popular legend gives a person with 15-5-8 one role: the traitor. The cards give at least four, and one person may play all of them over a lifetime. The scenes below are typical forms of the plot, not a prediction and not anyone's biography.

paragraphs.h3: The bound: the one who lives two lives

paragraphs: By day, a model family: the school parents' group chat, Sunday lunch with the in-laws, anniversary photos. By night, messages he deletes. Or a debt nobody at home knows about. Or betting, or a second flat. A double life rests not on a single passion but on the form: the more respectable the façade, the more the truth costs. Such a person wants the forbidden less than they are unable to discuss the permitted.
Wen makes an important caveat here: the Devil card “does not necessarily mean the Seeker is entirely to blame”. A chain is rarely forged alone.

paragraphs.h3: The keeper: the one who stays silent “for the family”

paragraphs: For thirty years a mother has held the house together on the rule “in our family people don't divorce”. She knows about her husband's second family and says nothing — for the children's sake, for grandmother's sake, for the sake of what the neighbours will say. Wen describes exactly this mechanism of the Hierophant: the good intention of shielding someone from the truth turns into harm, because “We are not the keeper of others.” The children grow up as keepers of a secret nobody ever entrusted to them, and learn that love and silence are the same thing.

paragraphs.h3: The judge: the one who keeps the account

paragraphs: After their father's death, the elder sister remembers everything: who put how much into the country house, who sat with father in his last year, who came once every six months. Her account is fair — and it never closes. Waite describes Justice as “the moral principle which deals unto every man according to his works”. But among its reversed meanings he lists “bigotry, bias, excessive severity”. Justice with no statute of limitations becomes the same Devil: a chain forged out of being right.

paragraphs.h3: The accused: the one appointed as the traitor

paragraphs: A son did not take over the family business. A daughter married someone who is “not one of us”. A brother left the community they all grew up in. There is no infidelity — only a refusal to conform, and the family judges it as betrayal. Wen writes that “with the pressure to conform comes persecution, often unfair persecution of others who have chosen not to conform”. In this role the Devil is not the person's sin but a label pinned on them. The history of the card itself shows that this has happened on a large scale too.

sections.h2: The Devil as an accusation: where the card got its goat's head
paragraphs: The familiar image of the Devil in tarot — a horned figure with a goat's head — is not ancient. Waite says so directly: “Since 1856 the influence of Éliphas Lévi and his doctrine of occultism has changed the face of this card, and it now appears as a pseudo-Baphometic figure with the head of a goat.” Lévi drew his Baphomet himself, for the book Dogme et Rituel de la Haute Magie (1854–1856). And he took the name from interrogation records.

On Friday, 13 October 1307, on the orders of King Philip IV of France, the Knights Templar were arrested across the country. They were charged with heresy and later with idol worship. In the interrogation records, where confessions were extracted under torture, the name Baphomet appears. The idol itself was never produced. Pope Clement V resisted at first, then ordered Templars arrested throughout Christendom, and in 1312 dissolved the order. On 18 March 1314 the Grand Master, Jacques de Molay, was burned in Paris — after he recanted his forced confession and declared the order innocent. Historians name money as one of the main reasons for the trial: the king needed funds, and the order was rich and independent.

Benebell Wen mentions this trial twice — under two of the tail's cards. The imagery of the Devil, she writes, is speculated to have been inspired by Baphomet, an idol the Templars purportedly worshipped. And she links the darker interpretation of the Hierophant to the theory that the card was inspired by Clement V. Both are hypotheses, not the established origin of the cards. But the plot with three parties is there: an accusation of devil worship, a pope, and a court. The Devil, the Hierophant and Justice.

For the tail, this leads to a simple and unpleasant point. **The Devil can be not only a sin but an accusation**, convenient for whoever is judging. In a 15-5-8 story it is worth asking not only “who betrayed?” but also “who gains from naming a traitor?”

sections.h2: 15-5-8 in relationships: vows, jealousy and a sentence with no end
paragraphs: Why is this tail read so often through love and family? The answer is in the scheme itself. Point M, the entry of the tail, also serves as the entry of the relationship line — the site's chart labels it exactly that: “entry of relationships and the tail”. So for everyone with 15-5-8, the relationship line also begins with the Devil. The same point sits in the energy column of Svadhisthana, the chakra of joy, children and creativity. And for people born in a year whose digits add up to 4, 13 or 22 (1966, 1975, 1984, 1993, 2002, 2011, 2020 and so on), the whole triple 15-5-8 stands both in the tail and on the relationship line. That is 11.5% of people with this tail.

A wedding — because it is time. A child — because everyone keeps asking. Divorce — out of the question, because “in our family people don't divorce”. The union rests on rules nobody chose, and it looks sturdier than many — until it turns out that its terms cannot be discussed. A Hierophant without the freedom to discuss is already half a Devil.

paragraphs.h3: Infidelity as a door, not a cause

paragraphs: In the logic of this tail, infidelity is not the start of the story but its middle: a way out of a union whose rules cannot be renegotiated out loud. If the honest door is locked by the form, a person leaves through the window — through a secret. So the conversation “why did you cheat?” often skips the main question here: why could nobody say earlier what was wrong? This is not an excuse for infidelity, but a pointer to where the circle could have been broken.

The other side of the same circle is a trial that starts without a crime. Checking a phone becomes an interrogation, a holiday together becomes a crime-scene reconstruction, and the partner lives as a suspect. Reversed Justice in Waite is “bias”. Jealousy in 15-5-8 is a verdict passed before the trial.

After an affair, a couple decides to stay together. Formally, forgiveness has happened; in fact, the case is still open: every late arrival is a new hearing, every quarrel goes back to that same year. The one who was forgiven lives on probation; the one who forgave has become a permanent prosecutor. Both feel cramped. Justice that knows no time limit becomes a chain for both sides.

The strong version of this tail in relationships is a union with an agreement spoken out loud. Fidelity in it is a choice that gets reaffirmed, not a chain that gets endured. The rules are revisited when life changes, and a break-up, if one is needed, goes through a conversation, not through a secret.

sections.h2: 15-5-8 in money and work: signatures, debts and golden handcuffs
paragraphs: In Waite and Wen, the Devil is attachment to the material, the Hierophant is the institution, Justice is law and contract. In work and money, the 15-5-8 circle runs just as it does in a family, only instead of a marriage there is an organisation, and instead of infidelity, a breach of the rules.

ul: **Golden handcuffs.** A high income at a company whose values the person does not believe in. Leaving is impossible: the mortgage, the status, “where else would they pay this much”. Service turns into servitude, and from outside it looks like a career.

**“That's how we do things here.”** A grey scheme the department considers normal. A signature on a document nobody reads. A bonus for something nobody mentions. The group norm (the Hierophant) covers the chain (the Devil) until an audit arrives (Justice).

**Money inside the family.** Loans to relatives without a receipt, co-signing a brother's loan, a flat registered in Mum's name, a family business run on a handshake. The agreement exists only in the parties' memories, and at the first conflict each side remembers it differently. A trial — family or real — is almost inevitable here.

**The mentor with the keys.** A boss, a teacher, a project lead everyone goes to for a decision — “the man to whom the Querent has recourse”, as Waite's list for the Hierophant puts it. If questions cannot be asked of him, the blessing has already been reversed.

paragraphs: This combination also has a very practical strong side. A person with 15-5-8 sees where an agreement turns into a trap, where a rule serves whoever wrote it, and where “that's how we do things” covers a violation. Lawyer, mediator, auditor, compliance specialist, notary, negotiator, addiction counsellor, author of internal policies, a mentor who is not afraid of questions — this is not a prediction of a profession, only examples of places where such an eye is needed.

sections.h2: Gretchen: the 15-5-8 circle Goethe described almost two hundred years before the matrix
paragraphs: Goethe knew nothing of the destiny matrix. All the more telling, then, that Gretchen's tragedy in the first part of Faust (1808) follows the 15-5-8 circle step by step. The quotations below are our own translations from the German.

**The Devil's gift and the Church's appetite.** Mephistopheles plants a casket of jewels for Gretchen. Her mother senses something wrong: “ill-gotten goods ensnare the soul” — in German “ungerechtes Gut”, literally “unjust goods”. She hands the find to a priest. He accepts it with pleasure: the Church, he says, has swallowed whole countries and never once overeaten, and “the Church alone can digest ill-gotten goods”. The Devil's gift disappears into the Hierophant, and nobody asks where it came from.

**The Hierophant's question.** In the garden, Gretchen asks Faust a direct question: “Now tell me, how do you stand on religion?” (“Nun sag, wie hast du's mit der Religion?”). In German it became an idiom: a “Gretchen question” (Gretchenfrage) is a question about the essential thing, one that cannot be answered evasively. Faust answers evasively.

**Betrayal out of love.** To meet at night, Gretchen gives her mother a sleeping draught she got from Faust: “What would I not do for your sake? I hope it will not harm her.” Her mother never wakes. Gretchen's brother Valentin dies in a duel with Faust and, dying, curses his sister in front of the whole street. The family betrayal here is committed not by a villain but by a girl in love who wanted to keep both her love and her respectability.

**The trial in the cathedral.** The most precise scene takes place in the cathedral. A service is under way (the Hierophant), an Evil Spirit whispers behind Gretchen's back (the Devil), and the choir sings the medieval hymn of the Last Judgement: “Judex ergo cum sedebit, quidquid latet adparebit, nil inultum remanebit” — “When the Judge takes his seat, all that is hidden will appear, nothing will remain unavenged” (Justice). All three cards of the tail meet in a single scene, and Gretchen faints.

**The horses and the trial.** At the end, Gretchen is in prison, sentenced to death. Faust comes to rescue her; outside, Mephistopheles is waiting: “My horses shudder, the morning is dawning.” Escape on the Devil's horses is the Chariot, the centre of the tail: riding away without untying anything. Gretchen refuses: “Judgement of God! To Thee I give myself up!” (“Gericht Gottes! dir hab ich mich übergeben!”). Mephistopheles declares: “She is judged!” (“Sie ist gerichtet!”). A voice from above replies: “She is saved!” (“Ist gerettet!”).

These last two lines illustrate Waite's idea about Justice exactly. He separates the moral law “which deals unto every man according to his works” from spiritual election, which is not handed out according to merit. Judged and saved is not a contradiction but two different courts. And one more detail. The only “handing over” in this story that destroys nothing is when Gretchen hands herself over to judgement instead of fleeing. The point is not to meekly accept any verdict of a family or a group. The point is that **the way out of the 15-5-8 circle begins not with escape but with a person ceasing to hide**.

sections.h2: Union or chain: how to tell them apart
paragraphs: From outside, a union and a chain are indistinguishable: the same dinners, signatures, vows and rules. The difference shows in a few signs. This is our reading, and it rests on “the liberty of service” — the thing, in Waite's words, the Devil is blind to.

ul: **The rules can be discussed.** In a union, the terms are revisited out loud when life changes. In a chain, there is one answer: “that's how it's done”.
**There is a way out without revenge.** A union that cannot be left without losing family, job or good name is held together by fear, not consent.
**The weak do not guard the secret.** If someone else's secret must be kept by those with less power — children, subordinates, juniors — it is a chain.

**The keys are not in one hand.** Waite's Hierophant is “the power of the keys”. When money, documents, passwords and information are gathered in one pair of hands and everyone else is left with trust, the form already works for the keyholder.
**Refusal is not counted as betrayal.** In service, a person can say “no” and still belong. In servitude, every “no” is recorded as betrayal.
**A sentence has an end.** A just decision names the act, the price and the end. A sentence with no end is no longer a trial but surveillance.

sections.h2: What to do with the 15-5-8 tail
paragraphs: A tail cannot be “closed” or “worked off” with a single action: the date of birth does not change. But the circle can be noticed and broken at any of its three links. The practices below are our reading of the cards, not a promise of results.

ol: **A census of vows.** Write down the rules a family or a team lives by: “in our family people don't divorce”, “money is men's business”, “we don't give up our own”. Next to each, note whose voice it is and when the rule was last discussed. A rule nobody remembers adopting is the first candidate for a chain.

**Agreements out loud.** Important arrangements — in relationships, with relatives, about money — should be spoken aloud and, where needed, written down. Set a review date: “let's come back to this in six months”. An agreement with a review date is a union. An agreement forever is a vow that will one day have to be broken.

**Secrets only between adults.** Do not make children the keepers of family secrets, the witnesses or the judges in adults' conflicts. Adult matters are settled between adults, with a specialist if necessary.
**Guilt is an act and a repair, not a life sentence.** Name the specific action and the specific amends. Forgiveness is a closed case, not a postponed one.

**No verdicts on the move.** The Chariot at the centre hurries things: decide, punish, leave today. Big decisions — a break-up, resigning, cutting off relatives — are made not at the peak of resentment but after a pause and a conversation.

**Leave through the door.** If a union is exhausted, leave openly: a conversation, a lawyer, a mediator, a fair division. A secret exit — through an affair, flight, disappearance — brings the person back into the circle through another entrance. An open exit may also feel like defeat: Wen calls this kind of release from former ties a spiritual Pyrrhic victory. The feeling does not prove the decision was a mistake.

**Test the hierophants.** A mentor, a boss, a spiritual teacher, a parent: can they be asked a question without the asker becoming an apostate? A teacher who cannot be questioned has already reversed his gesture.

**Do not stay alone with addiction, debts or threats.** This calls for specialists: a lawyer, a financial adviser, a psychologist, mutual-support groups. In case of violence or a threat to life, call a local emergency number or a local crisis line.

sections.h2: The strong side of 15-5-8: the one who knows chains from the inside
paragraphs: A tail named “Betrayal” has a rare strength. A person with 15-5-8 notices what others miss: where a union has become a chain, where a rule serves whoever wrote it, where a secret protects not the family but one of its members. This is knowledge from the inside — the way a noose is noticed by someone who was once caught in one.

The strong version of the tail is a person whose word holds because they gave it, not because they cannot take it back. A keeper of tradition who allows questions. A judge who remembers that a sentence must have an end. A mediator people bring family disputes to, because they do not take sides too early. The Chariot at the centre adds movement: the ability not only to see where the chain is, but to lead out of it.

Waite calls the Devil blind to the liberty of service. In the strong version of the tail, a person sees that liberty. **They are bound — but they choose their bonds themselves and can untie them by hand.** For this tail, loyalty and freedom stop being opposites.

sections.h2: What this reading is based on

ul: **Calculation** — the classic destiny matrix scheme: the tail is read in the order M–N–D, where D is the sum of day, month and year, E is the centre, M = D + E, N = D + M; numbers greater than 22 are reduced by adding their digits. The frequencies are our own count over all dates from 01.01.1900 to 31.12.2026.
**Card meanings** — A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1910; quoted from the 1922 reprint), parts I–III: The Devil, The Hierophant, Justice, The Chariot.
**Modern interpretation** — Benebell Wen, Holistic Tarot (2015): the chapters on Key 5, Key 7, Key 11 and Key 15.
**Numbering** — Marseille, as on the site's cards: 8 is Justice, 11 is Strength. In Waite and Wen these numbers are swapped; meanings are taken by the card's name.
**Words** — Vasmer's etymological dictionary of Russian (the entry for soyuz); the Bible (1 Cor 11:2 and 11:23; the Russian Synodal translation and the NRSV).

**Literature and history** — J. W. von Goethe, Faust, Part One (1808), the scenes “A Walk”, “Martha's Garden”, “Cathedral” and “Dungeon”, quoted in our own translation from the German; the trial of the Knights Templar (1307–1314).

**What is ours.** The circle of “chain — form — trial”, the four roles, the signs of a union and a chain, and the practices are our own synthesis based on the cards, not statements from the books. The past-life legend is given as a popular interpretation: it cannot be checked.

paragraphs: For a couple, 15-5-8 runs along the boundary between desire and obligation. Here the Devil is the entry to the task, the Hierophant, with promises and rules, is its middle, and Justice is the main task: owning decisions and one’s share of a mistake.

faq.q: What happened in a past life to a person with the 15-5-8 tail?
faq.a: The popular legend speaks of love triangles, affairs and a broken family, sometimes of a mentor who gave in to temptation. This cannot be checked: a date of birth gives no facts about past lives. The name “Betrayal in the Family” is better read through the cards: in Waite the Hierophant is marriage and alliance, the Devil is the chain, Justice is the trial. It describes a plot that may be playing out now, not a sentence for the past.

faq.q: Does the 15-5-8 tail mean that a person will be cheated on, or will cheat?
faq.a: No. The tail does not predict events and says nothing about the actions of any particular person. It describes the shape difficult stories tend to take: a union that cannot be discussed, a secret kept “for the family”, and a trial that never ends. Infidelity is just one possible form of this circle, and far from a necessary one.

No. In the classic scheme the tail is read in the order M–N–D, and the first number, M, is always a multiple of three: 3, 6, 9, 12, 15, 18 or 21. So an 8 can never come first, and 8-5-15 is not among the 26 tails the formula can produce. This notation appears when the tail is read bottom to top, from root to entry, or when the triple is taken for a “programme” in another position. The cards are the same, but in the 15-5-8 tail the entry is the Devil and the root is Justice, and they are not read the other way round.

faq.q: Is 15-5-8 on the relationship line the same as the tail?
faq.a: The cards are the same; the positions differ. The relationship line is read as M–R1–R, and its first point, M, is shared with the tail. In a worked example from one popular method — the date 15.07.1990 — the triple 15-5-8 stands precisely on the relationship line, while the tail of that date is a different one, 15-20-5. If the tail is 15-5-8 and the digits of the birth year add up to 4, 13 or 22, the triple 15-5-8 stands in both positions at once: this is true for 11.5% of people with this tail.

faq.q: How is 15-5-8 different from the tails 15-8-11 and 15-20-5?
faq.a: All three have the Devil at the entry; the mechanism and the root differ. In 15-5-8, Justice is the root, the returning question of “who owes whom”, and the mechanism is the Hierophant, the rule and the form. In 15-8-11, Justice becomes the mechanism and Strength goes to the root. In 15-20-5, the Hierophant becomes the root and Judgement the mechanism. Their centres differ too: 7, 4 and 10. So the same cards add up to different plots in these tails.

faq.q: Is the 15-5-8 tail different for men and women?
faq.a: No. In the classic scheme, sex does not change a single number, and the cards of the tail do not assign roles by gender. Anyone can turn out to be the bound one, the keeper, the judge or the accused in this plot.

There is no action after which the tail disappears: it is calculated from the date of birth. But the “chain — form — trial” circle can be broken at any link: by discussing the rules, by not keeping other people's secrets at the cost of one's own life, by giving sentences an end, by leaving openly rather than in secret. The strong version of the tail is not the absence of ties but bonds that are chosen consciously and can be revisited.

Do not label the child a future traitor or look for past-life sins in them. What follows from the cards is more useful: explain rules rather than just demanding obedience; allow questions; do not make the child the keeper of family secrets, a witness or a judge in adults' quarrels; punish for an act, and with a clear end. That way a child learns that rules can be discussed and love does not disappear because of it.

faq.q: Why is 8 Justice here and not Strength?
faq.a: The destiny matrix uses the Marseille numbering, in which 8 is Justice and 11 is Strength. In the Rider–Waite–Smith deck these two cards are swapped. The meaning of a card in a tail is taken by its name, so the root of 15-5-8 is Justice: the court, the law and judgement according to one's works.

It is one of the most common tails. Across all dates from 1900 to 2026 it occurs in 9.2% of cases, roughly one person in eleven, and ranks third out of 26, after 15-20-5 and 12-19-7. That is exactly why it matters not to speak of it as a sentence: such a large share of people cannot share one biography.

report: In Russian, betrayal and tradition grow from one root — predatelstvo and predanie — and the whole 15-5-8 tail lives between the two words. Popular readings call it “Betrayal in the Family” and explain the name with a past-life legend: love triangles, affairs, broken families. The legend cannot be checked: a date of birth says nothing about past lives. But the name does not rest on the legend alone. It is written into the cards themselves.

The cards of the tail are the Devil at the entry, the Hierophant as the mechanism and Justice at the root. Waite's divinatory list for the Hierophant opens with “Marriage, alliance, captivity, servitude”. He describes the Devil as “the chain and fatality of the material life”. Among the meanings of Justice is the “triumph of the deserving side in law”. **Marriage, chain, trial**: the legend can be put together almost word for word from the three cards. Only the legend speaks of one person who betrayed, while the cards speak of three figures: the one who is bound, the one who keeps the form, and the one who judges.

report.h3: The Devil is a Hierophant who is no longer free

report: Waite describes the Devil's raised hand as “the reverse of that benediction which is given by the Hierophant in the fifth card”. In his account, the Hierophant's gesture separates the manifest and the concealed parts of doctrine. The Devil makes the same gesture in reverse: the line between the manifest and the hidden remains, but now the hidden rules the manifest. Captivity is already present in the Hierophant himself — in Waite, marriage and captivity stand in the same line. Benebell Wen adds: “Hence, The Hierophant card is also about concealment.”

Of the Devil himself Waite writes: “blind to the liberty of service”. From outside, service and servitude look the same: the same loyalty, the same rules, the same person on top. **The Devil does not break into the family from outside. He is the family's own form, once it has stopped being free.**

Language keeps the same knot. From predat, “to hand over into someone else's hands”, come betrayal (predatelstvo), tradition with its family rules and faith (predanie), and the legal phrase predat sudu, “to commit to trial”. The three cards of the tail are one verb with three meanings. And the Old Russian sŭuzŭ meant both “fetters” and “union”.

report.h3: A sentence with no end is the same chain

report: The circle runs like this. An attachment appears that gives an immediate reward and takes away choice: passion, money, approval, a secret arrangement, a debt. It is hidden under a proper form — “that's how it's done”, “for the children's sake”, “what will people say” — or the form itself becomes the chain. The rules are no longer discussed: they are obeyed or secretly broken. Then what was hidden comes out, or an account builds up, and the trial begins: a divorce, a division of property, a family council, or an inner prosecutor who keeps the case open for years. A sentence that is too harsh gives birth to a new prohibition, and the prohibition to a new craving.

For thirty years a mother holds the house together on the rule “in our family people don't divorce” and says nothing about her husband's second family — for the children's sake. The children grow up as keepers of a secret nobody ever entrusted to them. After an affair, a couple stays together, but the case is still open: every late arrival is a new hearing. The one who was forgiven lives on probation; the one who forgave has become a permanent prosecutor. **Justice with no statute of limitations becomes the same Devil: a chain forged out of being right.**

In the logic of this tail, infidelity is not the start of the story but its middle: a way out of a union whose rules cannot be renegotiated out loud. If the honest door is locked by the form, a person leaves through the window — through a secret. It also happens the other way round: the “traitor” is someone who simply refused to conform — did not take over the family business, married someone who is “not one of us”. Then the Devil is not a sin but a label.

Everyone with 15-5-8 has the Chariot at the centre of the chart — the comfort zone. Waite writes the word “triumph” both for it and for Justice. Hence the temptation to turn a trial into a war, where the point is not to restore balance but to win. Or to leave: change city, job, partner. But the knot travels with the charioteer.

Goethe takes Gretchen in Faust through this circle step by step. A girl in love gives her mother a sleeping draught from Faust — “I hope it will not harm her” — and her mother never wakes. In the cathedral an Evil Spirit whispers behind Gretchen's back while the choir sings of the Last Judgement: “all that is hidden will appear”. At the end, Mephistopheles waits outside the prison: “My horses shudder, the morning is dawning.” Gretchen refuses to flee: “Judgement of God! To Thee I give myself up!” Mephistopheles declares: “She is judged!” A voice from above replies: “She is saved!” **The way out of the 15-5-8 circle begins not with escape but with a person ceasing to hide.**

report.h3: A union differs from a chain not in how tightly it holds, but in the right to renegotiate

report: From outside, a union and a chain are indistinguishable. In a union, the rules are revisited out loud, there is a way out without revenge, children and subordinates do not guard someone else's secret, “no” is not recorded as betrayal, and a sentence has an end. Hence the practices:

ul: speak agreements aloud and give them a review date;
do not make children the keepers of family secrets, the witnesses or the judges;
treat guilt as an act and a repair, not a life sentence;
make big decisions away from the peak of resentment;
if a union is exhausted, leave through the door — a conversation, a lawyer, a mediator — not through a secret;
in case of violence or a threat to life, call a local emergency number or a local crisis line.

report: The strong version of the tail is a person whose word holds because they gave it, not because they cannot take it back. A keeper of tradition who allows questions. A judge who remembers that a sentence must have an end. The Devil is blind to the liberty of service; in the strong version of 15-5-8, a person sees that liberty: **they choose their bonds themselves and can untie them by hand**.
